$CRDO just had a massive -20% day after its ER yesterday and I see a lot of people panicking, so let me give you my take.

Numbers first.

Record revenue of $479M, up 114.7%. EPS came in at $1.20 against $1.17. Q2 guided to $525-535M against $514.7M. FY27 growth guided above 85%, optical above $600M, gross margin at 68%. BofA cut its target from $340 to $275 and still kept the Buy.

So the print was good and the stock dropped 20%.

What got repriced was the slope.

Growth was 114.7% this quarter, the Q2 guide implies something like 96%, and the full-year guide says the second half slows down more. Every number is huge and every number is smaller than the one before it, and when you're priced for hyper-growth that's what people are actually paying for.

To me CRDO was never a buy, not because of the price, though at 140 I'd take the trade, but because I'd rather bet on the endgame than on a transition into it.

The most important part of my thesis is betting on the winners that make the future of AI happen, into 2030.

Energy: generation, and getting the electrons into the rack
AI Cloud: who owns the capacity and rents it out
AI Compute: the silicon, inference first
Memory: the real bottleneck, bandwidth and capacity next to the die
Interconnect: moving data where copper gives up

Credo doesn't sit cleanly in any of those, so I would only trade it, not go long on it.

Credo sells retimers and active electrical cables into the gap between copper and optics, and co-packaged optics is the thing that closes that gap. If CPO ramps faster than people expect in the 2027 architecture cycle, the products that got Credo here are the ones that get designed out. That's not a 2026 problem, but it's why a decelerating hyper-growth semi doesn't get to keep a 15x sales multiple forever. Throw in customer concentration, which is what hit the stock last time too.

At 165 you're paying around 12x forward sales for 85% growth at 68% gross margin, which honestly isn't expensive for an AI semi. At 140 it's 10x, and that's the level where even I'd take it as a trade.

Sub 160 is where I'd want it and 140 is where it gets genuinely cheap, though I wouldn't sit around waiting for that.

Not everyone has to share my take. 

A lot of people want to invest in the companies building the future right now, and CRDO is one of them.

Whatever you hold, hold it because of the thesis and not a change in price.

To me $CRDO's thesis didn't break and the stock got more attractive at these levels.

$NBIS is the one that hits closest to home for me.

Nvidia just told its biggest customers that servers with its AI chips are going up more than 15%, memory being the main driver. 

That squeeze lands on anyone who owns their GPUs on fixed-price contracts that aren't built yet. Revenue locked, hardware bill up. What separates the winners is contract structure, how short you run and how fast you can reprice. 

NBIS deliberately runs midterm and short-term deals and left 2027 capacity unsold specifically so it can reprice. New deals at $20m+/MW, short-term above $40m, and ~70% of Q2 bookings came prepaid covering half the capex. That's the pricing-power side of a winning company, not the locked-in-cheap side.

Goldman just moved their target to $328, up from $286. Buy reiterated.

After Q2 I raised my own base case to $353 from $329, bull case $475 to $560.

Yet the thing I keep coming back to is multiple compression. It's doing more damage to the math than dilution is, and people are overlooking it.

Business got better after Q2. Price round-tripped the whole thing anyway. $193 before earnings, $280 two days later, back to ~$210 today.

That's more interesting than it sounds. My base case didn't move at all. At $274 it was 29% upside, at $210 the same $353 is about 68%. Target held, entry got better.

And even in that base case, ARR more than triples and you still only get ~68%. Compression eats most of the growth. Almost nothing scaling to $11B of ARR keeps a 25x multiple, and the more capital intensive the business, the more certain that is.

Then there's dilution.

Nebius closed $5.75B of converts. Announced at $4.5B, priced at $5.0B, closed at $5.75B with the greenshoe taken in full. Strikes at $313.46 and $324.65.

My base case sits at $353, above both. So in my own base case both series convert and ~18M shares show up. Add the 15.8M Class A shares issued today swapping out the old 2029 and 2031 notes, and this one deal puts ~34M shares in play against a ~280M count.

Base and bull the converts turn into equity. It was never whether you get diluted. It's whether you get paid for it.

After the $SPCX IPO, the theme caught a lot of attention. So instead of chasing the name in the spotlight, I mapped the supply chain underneath it, from satellites down to minerals and everything in between.

The next space boom won't be won in space.

The global space economy hit $686B in 2025, up 12% in a year, with commercial activity at $544.3B of it. Space Foundation has it crossing $1.01 trillion by 2034.

Most of that money isn't made in space. Satellite-enabled products and services on the ground did $385.9B, roughly 71% of all commercial space revenue. Navigation, insurance, precision agriculture, logistics, aviation, broadband.

You think you have to be an astronaut to use these services? Think again. You're using them every day, in Google Maps.

Underneath that, the physical side is entering a real production phase. 2025 produced 317 orbital launches and 4,544 deployed spacecraft, up 25% and 54% versus 2024. Satellite manufacturing revenue grew 67.2%. Launch revenue grew 49.4%.

The line that matters most for this trade

Rockets got cheap and abundant. Launch infrastructure didn't keep up. Pads, ranges, integration facilities and coordination capacity have not moved anywhere near as fast as launch cadence.

Bottlenecks in an industrial buildout don't disappear. They migrate. Wherever the constraint lands next is where the pricing power goes.

That's the same reason I mapped twelve layers for AI. The visible company isn't always the bottleneck, and the best position usually sits a floor or two below the headline.

So here are the eight layers that are most relevant

L1 — Orbital Capacity, Data & Services. What customers actually buy. Broadband, mobility, earth observation, analytics, PNT, in-orbit services.

L2 — Networks, Fleets & Mission Operations. Constellations, mission control, capacity management, TT&C, data relay. Turning spacecraft into a service.

L3 — Finished Systems & Operational Assets. Launch vehicles, comms spacecraft, defense spacecraft, landers and servicers. The visible, qualified products.

L4 — Major Platform & System Elements. Launch stages, fairings and dispensers, spacecraft buses, payload modules.

L5 — Functional Subsystems & Assemblies. Propulsion and fluids, structures and mechanisms, power and thermal, avionics and GNC, payload assemblies.

L6 — Components, Electronics & Precision Parts. Compute and avionics, RF and interconnect, photonics and optics, propulsion hardware, structural and thermal. This is where the hidden bottlenecks live. A cheap part that can't be qualified delays an entire mission.

L7 — Engineered Materials & Mill Forms. Superalloys, composites, ablatives, electronic and optical materials, mill stock.

L8 — Critical Raw Materials. Structural and refractory metals, ceramics, semiconductor materials, rare earths, battery materials. This is what determines availability, geopolitical exposure, and the economics of expanding anything above it.

And four rails running alongside

Some capabilities don't sit inside the stack, they run beside it, and they can become bottlenecks in their own right.

Launch Services & Infrastructure. Pads, towers, propellant farms, integration facilities, range safety, recovery assets. The clearest evidenced bottleneck in the sector right now, and almost nobody has it on a list.

Ground Segment & User Access. Gateways, user terminals, mission control, network core. A gateway isn't made from satellites and a satellite isn't made from gateways, which is exactly why it gets filed under support infrastructure and ignored.

Manufacturing, Test & Qualification. Five-axis machining, autoclaves, thermal-vacuum chambers, vibration test, antenna ranges, engine test stands, radiation screening. Anyone can add a machine. Adding a machine whose output is certified to fly takes years.

Propellants & Consumables. LOX, methane, kerosene, hydrazine, xenon, krypton. Demand scales with how often you fly, not how many vehicles come off the line.

The honest part

With AI I have an unfair advantage. I run AI at a major enterprise, so I'm the customer and my suppliers tell me where the next constraint is forming before it shows up in a headline.

Space isn't my day job, I wish it was. What I have is a network inside the biggest space companies in the world and a framework, and the framework travels.

Also worth saying, the biggest blind spot in this map is vertical integration. At least one major player builds most of its own stack, and every layer it absorbs is a supplier that stops existing. A layered map is architecturally incapable of showing that. It's the weakness in my own framework and probably the most important competitive fact in the industry.

Even after being reviewed by friends who work at NASA and SpaceX, this can still be improved.

After the drawdown, it sits 33% off its all-time high, an opportunity that’s hard to pass up.

Penguin doesn’t make the accelerator and doesn’t make the DRAM. It takes raw memory from manufacturers and packages it into custom modules built to spec, then stands up the clusters those modules go into. Whoever wins the socket, whoever wins the model, the boxes still get built and the memory still gets integrated.

This is why I like this company so much:

The memory business is not a segment anymore; IT IS THE COMPANY. Integrated Memory did $275 million last quarter and more than doubled year over year. That is 57% of a business that printed record net sales of $479 million, up 48%. GAAP operating income of $51 million, up 417%. GAAP diluted EPS of $0.68 against a one cent loss a year ago. Management raised full year guidance on both sales and EPS off the back of it.

Advanced Compute looks flat, $137.6 million against $132.5 million. The non-hyperscale piece, enterprise and sovereign and neoclouds, grew 81% year over year and is now 60% of that segment. The flat line is a deliberate pivot out of low margin hyperscaler work. The mix shift is hiding the growth. Hyperscalers build in house and always will. Everyone below them cannot, and there are more of them every quarter.

They have already proven they can execute at sovereign scale. The Haein cluster with SK Telecom, over 1,000 Blackwell GPUs, 50-plus miles of precision-laid fiber, integrated into SK Broadband’s Gasan data center. Order placement to go-live in two months. That is one of the fastest deployments of an AI supercomputing system at that scale that anyone has done.

Management is getting a serious upgrade. Mark Papermaster, the sitting CTO of AMD. Penny Herscher, who also chairs Lumentum. And now David Heard, who ran Infinera before Nokia bought it and who now leads Nokia’s Network Infrastructure division. Memory, CPU and photonics all sitting at the same nine person table.

The photonics leg is the optionality we get almost for free. Penguin called photonics early and was in Celestial AI before Marvell bought it. They are now building the Photonic Memory Appliance, a box that uses light to link memory across servers so an entire cluster shares one pool like it is one machine. IF it works it is the highest margin and most defensible IP in the company and nothing in the multiple reflects it. If it slips I still own a profitable memory and integration business.

The risks are here as with any growth stock

The cluster business is lumpy and one customer sliding a quarter wrecks the print. It already happened. Q2 was down 42% year over year. 

Cash conversion is thin. $11 million of operating cash flow year to date against record earnings, carried by a payables build. Record profit and weak cash in the same quarter is a thing I watch closely.

Part of Q3 net income came from equity investment disposals. Operating income was $51 million and net income landed at $44.7 million. Clean until you look at the mix.

High DRAM prices cut both ways. Great for the memory segment, and they also slow customer orders and squeeze gross margin.

Their photonics angle is a 2027 story. If it slips this sits dead money for a while.

The memory business is compounding right now, the growth in Advanced Compute is real and buried under a mix shift, they have already delivered a sovereign cluster in two months, and the board is built for a company three sizes larger than the one the market is pricing.

Execution is everything from here. 

Sovereign and enterprise AI spending has not ramped yet, and that spend is less cyclical than hyperscaler capex, which may peak in 2028.
